output.myth: Ennu the Kite-Wright found a plank on the north beach, split down its length where a boat had broken on the rocks. His youngest sister wanted to fly, and there was no cloth fit for it, so he lashed the wood into a frame and stretched sailcloth across it, one knot at each corner. The wind came in off the water and took it up, and she screamed with joy and did not want to give the string back. Hesk watched from the pole and said nothing. When the girl grew old and went aloft herself, Ennu would not burn the frame, and it would not burn anyway. So he hung it in the Spindle on a cord of Hesk's own thread, where no gale can reach it. Each winter Tavo the Gale rattles the house-poles, and the frame stays put. Mothers tie a scrap of red cloth to the knot at its foot before a child first flies, so the wind knows whose it is.
output.verse:
Split plank on the shore,
Ennu lashed the frame and cloth,
Hung where gales cannot.
